extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Renaissance literature (Rabelais), general readers of Gargantua
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading/annotation of an English translation excerpt from Rabelais' Gargantua and Pantagruel that contains both narrative and extended prescriptive passages (education, law, disputation). Useful for literary scholars, teachers, and readers analyzing rhetorical and prescriptive elements in Renaissance satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language mastery (learn the languages perfectly)
rubrics_metrics.description: “that thou learn the languages perfectly; first of all the Greek, as Quintilian will have it; secondly, the Latin; and then the Hebrew, for the Holy Scripture sake; and then the Chaldee and Arabic likewise”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also instructs to "frame thy style in Greek in imitation of Plato, and for the Latin after Cicero." Emphasises perfect learning of these tongues as foundational to scholarship; languages are treated as prerequisites for understanding law, scripture, and antiquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive liberal arts curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation to pursue the liberal arts: "Of the liberal arts of geometry, arithmetic, and music, I gave thee some taste ... Proceed further in them, and learn the remainder if thou canst. As for astronomy, study all the rules thereof."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the classical quadrivium and trivium areas recommended; study astronomy's rules but explicitly "Let pass, nevertheless, the divining and judicial astrology, and the art of Lullius, as being nothing else but plain abuses and vanities." (antipattern: avoid magical/fortune-telling branches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural history and encyclopaedic knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: "I would have thee to study that exactly, and that so there be no sea, river, nor fountain, of which thou dost not know the fishes; all the fowls of the air; all the several kinds of shrubs and trees ... all the sorts of herbs and flowers ... all the various metals ... together with all the diversity of precious stones"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A demand for exhaustive empirical knowledge of nature: 'Let nothing of all these be hidden from thee.' Presented as part of a model of complete scholarship—memorisation and acquaintance with natural particulars are virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical and anatomical study
rubrics_metrics.description: "Then fail not most carefully to peruse the books of the Greek, Arabian, and Latin physicians, not despising the Talmudists and Cabalists; and by frequent anatomies get thee the perfect knowledge of the other world, called the microcosm, which is man."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates comparative reading across medical traditions and hands‑on anatomical practice. Emphasises anatomy as key to knowledge of humanity (the 'microcosm'), and recommends openness to diverse sources (even Talmudists and Cabalists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural study and moral formation
rubrics_metrics.description: "At some hours of the day apply thy mind to the study of the Holy Scriptures; first in Greek, the New Testament, with the Epistles of the Apostles; and then the Old Testament in Hebrew."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural learning goes with moral injunctions: "Knowledge without conscience is but the ruin of the soul." Recommends piety: 'serve, love, fear God,' suspect worldly abuses, love neighbours, reverence teachers, and shun bad company. Moral formation is integral to the scholarly programme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical martial training
rubrics_metrics.description: "as thou growest great and becomest a man, thou must part from this tranquillity and rest of study, thou must learn chivalry, warfare, and the exercises of the field"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars are expected to acquire martial and practical skills to defend household and friends; learning is not purely theoretical but also prepares for active civic/military duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public disputation as test of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: "I will that very shortly thou try how much thou hast profited, which thou canst not better do than by maintaining publicly theses and conclusions in all arts against all persons whatsoever"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates publicly defending theses and engaging learned company (Paris and elsewhere) as the way to prove and sharpen learning. The passage describes Pantagruel setting up thousands of conclusions and disputing at length—presented as the rigorous standard of scholarly competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct oral testimony over voluminous records in adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantagruel's judicial principle: "Is it not better to hear their controversy from their own mouths whilst they are face to face before us, than to read these vile fopperies ... these records ... were but engines wherewith to overthrow justice"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a method for resolving complex disputes, the text advocates discarding piles of legal writings (which are depicted as obfuscatory) and instead convening the parties to speak directly. Pantagruel even proposes burning the papers—an extreme anti‑procedure against prolix legalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding law requires classical languages and philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertion that "the laws are excerpted out of the middle of moral and natural philosophy ... the laws are so full that without it they cannot be understood" and criticism that many jurists lacked Greek/Latin knowledge
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that proper legal interpretation depends on knowledge of Greek and Latin and on philosophical learning; legal commentators who lack these foundations are caricatured as 'blockheads' whose styles are unfit for juridical understanding.
